thesis.headline: Leland is [the home for ambition]. Get there, with the people who've been there.
body: Leland exists to help ambitious people get where they’re going, and the brand's job is to make getting ahead feel human, not transactional. Most ambitious people don't know anyone who has done the thing they want to do, so they guess from anonymous threads and polished highlight reels. Leland puts real people with real names and verified backgrounds in front of them, years before they'd normally have that kind of network.

The 2026 rebrand (Leland 2.0, launched June 15, 2026) started from an honest diagnosis: the old brand was weak and generic, didn't inspire the ambition we know we can, and its green diamond logo wasn't ownable. The refresh rethought positioning, visual identity and tone together, and the only thing off the table was the name. The ask was to grow up a little, feel more human, and make people feel Leland is on their side.

The vibe is a brilliant friend who takes your ambitions seriously, or the older sibling who shows up exactly when the goal starts to feel real but the path still feels unclear. Warm but not soft, aspirational but not intimidating, exclusive but not elitist. The biggest goals should feel closer after visiting Leland, not further away.

That is why it looks the way it does: mostly ink, grey and white, with a single blue reserved for the phrase that matters, a serif (Season) for the headline and a clean sans (Macan) for everything else, real photography of real people, and a thin blue line illustration when a photo would say too much. Cover the logo and you should still know it's Leland, in the copy, the visuals and the tone. Nothing here looks like a generic gradient, a stock photo or a Silicon Valley startup template.

It is a two-sided brand. To people chasing a goal it has to feel aspirational and trustworthy; to the experts building a business on Leland it has to feel professional and worth their name. Both audiences matter equally, and trust is earned through transparency: real reviews, real outcomes, real pricing.

principles.name: Human, not corporate
principles.desc: There are real people on both sides of every interaction, and everything we make should feel that way.

principles.name: Warm but not soft
principles.desc: We care deeply about the people we serve, and we also believe in pushing them toward something hard, because ambition isn't comfortable.

principles.name: Aspirational but not intimidating
principles.desc: The biggest goals should feel closer after visiting Leland, not further away.

principles.name: Exclusive but not elitist
principles.desc: Experts are vetted and outcomes are real, but the door is open to anyone willing to do the work, at a range of price points.

principles.name: Trust through transparency
principles.desc: Real reviews, real names, real outcomes and real pricing do the persuading, so we never invent a number or a testimonial.

principles.name: Distinctive, not generic
principles.desc: Cover the logo and you should still know it's Leland, in a category full of generic gradients and stock photography.

voice.summary: Direct, concrete, confident and warm, like a smart friend who has done it and is telling you how, never hyped and never shouting.
sounds_like: Lead with the point, no throat-clearing, short sentences and strong verbs.
Every claim has a number, a named company, a named school or a real person behind it.
Warm comes from the invitation: come ask, the door's open, send this to someone who needs it.
Confident, not excited: the brand doesn't use exclamation points outside verbatim quotes.
Headlines in sentence case, 4 to 8 words, usually leading with a verb.
Sells what you'll be able to do and how fast, as in outcome plus timeframe.
Talks to a smart, busy reader who has read enough marketing to be skeptical.
not_like: LinkedIn highlight-reel posturing or networking for networking's sake.
Corporate training-module language or motivational poster filler.
Tech-startup jargon that describes the product as AI-powered, algorithmic or personalized.
Treating the audience as behind or ignorant, since people arrive informed.
Hedging, passive voice and vague encouragement with no instruction.
words_we_use: people who've done it, people who've been there
come ask, follow along, send this to someone
your feed is built around your goal
specific names: Google, Goldman, McKinsey, Bain, HBS
get there, get in, land the offer
words_we_avoid: coach, coaching (say expert, session, book time)
unlock, empower, elevate, transform, journey, navigate, landscape
leverage, ensure, streamline, seamless, holistic, robust, synergy
platform, ecosystem, revolutionize, game-changer, cutting-edge, world-class
AI-powered, AI-driven, personalized, algorithm (for the Community product)
thought leaders, industry professionals, top companies with no examples
join our community, find your tribe
Thrilled to announce, I'm humbled, Welcome to the era of, Let's dive in
em dashes and exclamation points in Leland's own copy

dos: Lead with learning from people who've done it; meeting peers is a bonus, not the headline.
Name the company, the school, the number or the person; if you can name it, do.
Put the one phrase that matters in blue and leave everything else ink.
Use Season only for the headline and Macan for everything else.
Use real photography of real, relatable people from normal companies and schools, not elite-only personas.
Write headlines in sentence case, 4 to 8 words, no period unless the period is the move.
Make the CTA a verb: Come ask, Follow along, Book a session, Enroll now.
Quote testimonials verbatim, punctuation and all, with Name · Detail attribution.
Say experts post with real names, not every post.
Back every bit of launch energy with something real: a specific question, company or person.
donts: Don't use the old green brand, the green compass diamond, Calibre or Inter; that brand is dead.
Don't show the logomark in yellow, and don't make the logo the hero of a layout.
Don't introduce a second accent color or a cream, beige, orange or green background.
Don't put more than one blue phrase on a surface or let blue become a fill.
Don't use exclamation points, em dashes or title-case headlines in Leland's own copy.
Don't call the Community product AI-powered, personalized or algorithmic.
Don't name LinkedIn as the comparison in public posts; show the difference and let readers draw it.
Don't make up numbers, quote sample numbers from graphics as real, or invent a testimonial.
Don't use stock photos, generic gradients, confetti textures or placeholder avatars.
Don't write subcopy, helper lines or status notes under a heading; a heading stands alone.

audience.name: Ambitious student (core)
audience.desc: A sophomore at a business school in a top-50 university, eyeing consulting, finance, product or tech, who knows they need to network but doesn't know where to start.

audience.name: Grad school applicant
audience.desc: An MBA, law or med applicant who worries their background doesn't fit and wants to hear from someone who got in with a profile like theirs.

audience.name: Career switcher or early professional
audience.desc: Someone whose goal has started to feel real while the path still feels unclear, and who wants the inside track without the elite network.

audience.name: Existing Leland client
audience.desc: A paying customer who wants more value between sessions through questions, livestreams, AMAs and more experts.

audience.name: AI Builder Program student or grad
audience.desc: A professional learning to build with AI who wants a place to show what they built and see what the cohort is shipping.

audience.name: Leland expert
audience.desc: A vetted professional building an audience and a business on Leland, who needs the brand to feel professional and worth attaching their real name to.

audience.name: Teams and enterprise buyers
audience.desc: Companies buying AI training or hiring from the ambitious people on Leland, who read for security, ROI and rollout rather than hype.

visual.type: Season (serif, weight 500) is for headlines and large sizes only, roughly 32px and up; Macan carries body, UI, captions, buttons and post cards. Never substitute Georgia, Inter or Calibre; a stand-in serif reads as off-brand.
visual.color: Monochrome first: ink #111111 for text, #4c4c4c and #767676 for secondary text, #f5f5f5 grey and white paper for surfaces. One accent blue #2f5fd6 marks the single phrase that matters; soft blue #80aced is for line illustrations and the occasional full-bleed panel; yellow #ffd667 appears sparingly as a small accent and never on the logomark. No green, cream, beige, orange or a second accent.
visual.photography: Real people, real settings, candid and a little grainy, with motion and natural light; relatable subjects from normal companies and schools rather than elite-only personas. Photography is the only thing allowed as a background image, usually under a soft white-to-dark gradient so ink or white type stays legible.
visual.illustration: Thin single-weight line drawings in soft blue #80aced on white, like a hand-drawn pathway or diagram. Use them when a photo would say too much or when the idea is abstract (a goal, a path, a feed); never fill them, never add a second color, and never mix them with icon-style category graphics.
visual.logo: The Leland 2.0 logomark is the black slanted-L mark; the lockup is logomark plus the Leland wordmark set in Macan. Use black on light, white on dark, and never yellow, never green, never the old compass diamond. Keep it small and quiet in the top-left of a layout; the logo is a signature, not the hero.
visual.motion: Text animates one of three ways: Typed (characters arrive one by one, cursor-less), Rise (lines rise and fade in, staggered) or Words (each word scales in, staggered), and the blue phrase stays blue throughout. The logo intro is Leo spins in: the loader spins, the ears land and the mark settles into the wordmark, followed by a tagline such as Get there, with the people who've been there and the store badges. Launch videos live in a white void with product UI, one blue-highlighted phrase and this outro.

A June 2026 launch thread chose a yellow background behind the logo for social profile pictures; the standing rule is that the logomark itself is never yellow, so treat that as a profile-picture exception, not a logo color.

Company Values says 'We exist to unlock human potential' and the Series A messaging used 'unlock human potential in new ways'; house-style bans 'unlock' in Leland copy, so quote the mission verbatim when needed but do not write new copy with it.

Lebrain brand foundations guide is noted as incomplete as of June 2026; no finished written brand guideline for Leland 2.0 was found, so principles here are compiled from the kickoff, house style and the marketing copy guide.
